phase: C5 -- future_outcome reveal, retrospective stress test ONLY
principle: future_outcome is NOT ground truth for historical startup quality. Used only to ask: given what was knowable at the snapshot, did SIE identify meaningful strengths/risks that later proved relevant? SIE is not punished for failing to predict genuinely unknowable future events. No score was altered after this reveal.

companies.future_outcome: Failure/fire sale -- sold to PCH International in 2015 for a small fraction of its former $1B valuation; effective shutdown (2015-01).
companies.retrospective_finding: Strong validation. The crisis narrative that drove the lowest score in the holdout set (Series D shortfall, two rounds of substantial layoffs, a key co-founder's departure at the pivot) was real, dated, well-corroborated pre-snapshot evidence -- and it directly anticipated the eventual failure. Not a lucky guess: the specific facts cited are the same category of facts that precede failure generally.

companies.future_outcome: Bankruptcy, November 2015; Pandora acquired its technology assets for $75M. Outcome summary explicitly attributes this to being 'unable to close the funding and scale gap with Spotify and other well-capitalized competitors.'
companies.retrospective_finding: Direct validation of the single most decisive dimension score in this holdout run: Competitive Intensity (scored 2, materially weak) was built entirely from the contemporaneous, quantified H1-2012 Spotify revenue/valuation comparison -- and the eventual failure's stated proximate cause is exactly that competitive/scale gap. SIE identified the specific risk factor that later proved decisive, using only publicly knowable, pre-snapshot evidence.

companies.future_outcome: Shutdown, July 2015, citing inability to raise further funding amid worker-misclassification lawsuits AND 'persistently poor customer retention/repeat-usage rates that undermined its economics.'
companies.retrospective_finding: Partial, notable validation plus one genuine blind spot. VALIDATED: SIE's blind Unit Economics score (3, Weak, from the $20/hour-vs-contractor-cost tension) and its explicit flagging that Retention data was conspicuously absent for a recurring-service business both directly anticipated the 'poor retention... undermined its economics' finding -- this is a real, evidence-grounded, non-lucky anticipation of the actual failure driver. NOT VALIDATED / GENUINE BLIND SPOT: the worker-misclassification lawsuits are not represented anywhere in the pre-snapshot evidence SIE had access to, and the current 28-dimension architecture has no dimension whose explicit purpose is labor/employment-classification legal risk. Per instruction, SIE is not penalized for this -- it is logged as a possible future-methodology consideration (see failure analysis), not a defect.

companies.future_outcome: Became the largest U.S. food-delivery platform by market share; $535M Series D at $1.4B (2018); IPO December 2020 at a valuation exceeding $60 billion.
companies.retrospective_finding: The most important case for the 'do not punish for unknowable future events' principle. DoorDash's blind SPS sits near the bottom of the holdout set (essentially tied with Rdio, which failed), yet the company became an extraordinary success. This is explicitly NOT read as a SIE failure: the March 2016 snapshot evidence was genuinely thin and cautionary on its own terms -- a flat valuation despite a larger raise (a real, standard venture caution signal), a crowded field of several similarly-well-funded rivals (Postmates, Caviar, UberEats), no claimed technical differentiation, no disclosed traction. Several of DoorDash's 2016-era competitors did NOT go on to dominate the category -- DoorDash's eventual outsized outcome depended on years of subsequent execution, capital access, and competitive attrition that had not yet occurred and was not evidenced at the snapshot date. Also notable: DoorDash's evidence coverage (21.4%) was the lowest in the holdout set, tied with Rdio -- the coverage metadata itself honestly signals 'this is a low-confidence read,' which is exactly the correct behavior: a viewer would not be misled into treating 46.8 as a confident negative prediction. This is a genuinely unknowable-future-event case (category J), not a scoring defect.

companies.future_outcome: Systematic compliance scandal -- the company had enabled brokers to bypass state-mandated insurance-licensing training. CEO Parker Conrad resigned Feb 2016; valuation halved to $2B; large layoffs; 'never recovered its earlier trajectory.'
companies.retrospective_finding: The explicit test case, and the clearest illustration of the instruction's principle. SIE's blind score (highest in the holdout set) accurately reflects what was genuinely, publicly, verifiably strong about Zenefits at the snapshot: a real, extraordinary, well-documented 9x valuation step-up in one year, backed by sophisticated institutional investors (Fidelity, TPG). This was not a scoring error -- it was an accurate read of real public information. The catastrophic outcome stemmed from an internal, actively-concealed compliance practice that was not disclosed and not knowable from any public source as of the snapshot date -- close to definitionally outside what a public-evidence-based methodology can see, regardless of dimension design. Non-punitive structural observation: the current 28 dimensions have no dimension explicitly aimed at regulatory/compliance/governance integrity (Leadership covers hiring/org-building; Execution Track Record covers milestone achievement; neither covers 'is growth being achieved through means that create latent legal/reputational risk'). This is logged as a candidate topic for a future Methodology v2.1 conversation -- NOT as a v2 defect, since no public-evidence architecture could have surfaced concealed internal misconduct.

cross_cutting_observation: Both Rdio and Fab.com show the same pattern: a real, dated, public, decisive risk factor was correctly identified blind and later proved to be the actual proximate cause of failure. Homejoy shows a partial version of the same pattern (unit-economics/retention correctly flagged; a legal-risk driver was not, and could not have been, evidenced). DoorDash and Zenefits both illustrate the instruction's central caution against hindsight bias, from opposite directions: DoorDash shows that thin, cautious, evidence-grounded scoring is not a failure when a genuinely uncertain situation later resolves favorably through means not yet knowable; Zenefits shows that an accurate reflection of genuinely strong public evidence is not a failure when a later-discovered concealed practice changes the outcome.
